## THE FAILURE STORY

It started cleanly enough. You merged the first batch of commits from claimgate/bypass-regression into a feature branch, expecting to sequence them by date. Commits 1–8 landed without file conflicts. system_v5 tests passed. But when you merged commit 12 (from worktree 7, modifying CB library initialization), the code compiled, the linter passed, and git declared it clean. You committed it.

Then the integration tests failed. Commit 9 (from worktree 3, which you'd already merged) called `CBLibrary.init_boundary()` with three arguments. But commit 12 had rewritten that function to take five arguments and moved it to a different module. No file conflict meant git saw no problem—the two changes were in different files. But the dependency was real, and it was now broken. By the time you discovered this, you'd already merged commits 14–19, each of which layered more assumptions on top of the broken state. Unwinding meant reverting six commits and re-merging in a different order. But commits 14–16 touched the same system_v7 files as commit 12, so re-merging 12 first meant re-resolving those conflicts by hand. Meanwhile, the primary checkout's 180 dirty files (experimental work on claimgate/bypass-regression) were never staged, so you couldn't stash them cleanly. You ended up with a diverged local state: a test branch heading one way, uncommitted work heading another, and no clear path to merge everything back to main.

By the time you mapped out the actual dependency graph (commit 3 → 12 → 14; commit 8 → 21; commit 9 → 28 → 35), you had lost two days and had three broken intermediate states in git history.

## THE UNDERLYING ASSUMPTION

Commits that merge without file conflicts are semantically compatible.

## EARLY WARNING SIGNS

1. First batch of merged commits passes file-level tests but fails integration tests with undefined-reference or function-signature errors from commits not yet merged.

2. Commit message or code review notes mention "assumes X is already in the codebase" or "pending the CB boundary refactor"—a signal that the commit depends on work in another worktree, but that dependency is undeclared.
